Introduction/Concepts

Development guide

Concepts

An AI coding agent can produce a working change that solves the wrong problem or misses an important constraint. This page explains how clear goals, relevant information, suitable tools and feedback help teams direct and check its work.

An AI agent uses a model to choose or adapt actions and tool use towards a goal, within agreed permissions and limits. A workflow can combine agents with predefined code paths and automated checks. The concepts below explain how to define the task, support the agent and review its work. [9]

The examples assume familiarity with requirements, code changes and tests. These practices support work throughout the lifecycle. Start with the relationship map, then follow the reading route or choose the concept that addresses your current problem.

AIHow AI can help in this chapter

  • Clarify intent and specifications
  • Use context and tools
  • Improve and coordinate work
  • Compare models

How the concepts fit together

Building a change with an AI agent involves more than asking it to write code. The team needs to agree what would help users, describe the expected behaviour, give the agent information and tools, and decide what happens after each check.

Worked exampleFictional scenarioFollow one application through every conceptSee how each concept contributes to Maya’s asset-management application, the case used across this guide.

Maya manages a project’s laptops, monitors and docking stations in a spreadsheet. Members tell her about handovers, faults and losses by message, so the register falls out of date and she spends time chasing updates. The team investigates the causes and compares a managed form, an existing asset platform and a custom application. For the example, it chooses an application in which members record acknowledged handovers, report faults or losses and complete an annual declaration. Project Discovery follows the full case.

AI agents help draft requirements, change code and run checks. Application code enforces one rule that connects the examples: each asset has exactly one current holder, and a handover completes only when the receiving member acknowledges it, including when the same acknowledgement arrives twice at once. AI supports development; the application does not need an AI model to enforce this rule.

The table uses this guide’s working definitions to show each concept’s contribution. Model choice and other decisions can be revisited as the work changes.

How each concept contributes to the fictional asset-management application
ConceptContribution to the application
IntentThe team investigates why Maya’s register falls out of date, agrees the intended outcome and carries that agreement into implementation and review.
SpecificationCriteria define handover acknowledgement, fault and loss reports, annual declarations, access and service failures. Two simultaneous acknowledgements cannot leave an asset with two current holders.
ContextThe developer supplies asset and handover rules, the asset API contract, relevant code and tests. Conflicting rules need a recorded decision before implementation continues.
HarnessAn editor, terminal, browser and isolated test database let the agent change code and exercise handover behaviour. Permissions and run records bound and explain its actions.
Feedback loopsA concurrent-handover test exposes a defect. The agent corrects the code within agreed limits; the developer can separately evaluate revised instructions for future tasks.
Verification engineeringThe team states the rule before the agent starts, derives the expected answer independently and chooses a check strong enough for the risk, from one example to a property or model check.
Workflow dependenciesAfter the build passes, specialist agents check functionality, permissions and architecture on the same commit. Combined findings determine correction, escalation or human review.
Agentic development environmentOne place to see several agent tasks at once: which handover, form and declaration tasks are running, what each agent has changed, where work is blocked and what needs a decision. Each task keeps its own branch, workspace and evidence until review.
Persistent agentA fault-triage agent works through new fault reports overnight, starts a coding-agent session for each confirmed defect and brings decisions to the product owner. It cannot merge, deploy or read production member records.
Software factoryThe delivery workflow connects agreed asset-management changes to checks, review, release authority and monitoring. Failed handovers, missed declarations and user feedback become follow-up work.
Model selectionThe developer compares models on representative asset-management tasks using the same tools and checks. Correctness, correction effort, time, cost and data handling inform the choice.

A failed check can expose an unresolved decision. If the team has not agreed whether members may submit an annual declaration after its due date, another code retry will not settle that question. The product owner resolves the expected behaviour; the developer records the decision and updates the criteria and task context before the agent continues.

How far to delegate each task is a separate decision from which practices to apply. The agentic coding maturity reference describes the L0–L5 levels of delegation, what a person still reads at each level, and the verification each climb requires; this page teaches the practices that make each climb safe.

Agree the goal (intent-driven development)

Intent-driven development makes the intended outcome, behaviour and constraints explicit and keeps them available as AI-assisted work progresses. Start by agreeing why a change is needed, then carry that intent through planning, implementation and review.

Use it when a request leaves room for conflicting interpretations. “Improve asset tracking” could mean easier reporting, fewer chasing messages or reliable handover records. Agree the user need before asking an agent to implement a solution.

Agree the outcome and constraints

  • Problem: who is affected, and what prevents them from completing their task?
  • Outcome: what should the user be able to do after the change?
  • Constraints: which access rules, data-handling requirements or existing behaviours need to remain?
  • Open questions: what is undecided, who will resolve it and when is the decision needed?
Worked exampleFictional scenarioDefine the outcome before choosing a solutionSee how a team connects a record-keeping problem to the outcome it wants to improve.

The team investigates why Maya’s asset register falls out of date before choosing what to build:

  • Problem: members report handovers, faults and losses by message, and the register names people who no longer hold the equipment.
  • Outcome: Maya can rely on the register, and members can report changes when they happen.
  • Constraints: each asset has one current holder; members can change only their own assets and handovers unless separately authorised.
  • Open question: is the difficulty caused by the missing reporting route or by asset identifiers people cannot match to equipment? The product owner compares observations of both before selecting an improvement.

AI can organise the findings and suggest options. Members try the proposed workflow; the product owner records where they find an asset, complete a report or need help. Those observations inform the choice between a managed form, an existing platform and building an application.

After choosing the application, the team keeps the outcome and supporting evidence with its requirements. Later tests check handover behaviour; user observations are still needed to assess whether the application solves the original problem.

Keep the record proportionate

A short issue may be enough for a small defect. A new capability may need research and a product requirements document. Recording a goal does not establish that it is valuable; test important assumptions before committing substantial effort.

AIHow AI can help

Ask AI to group employee feedback and link proposed findings to the original notes. The product owner compares decision-relevant findings with those notes, checks contradictory or duplicated evidence and records unsupported explanations as open questions. Use those questions to choose the next observation or prototype test.

Next step: Write the problem, outcome and constraints for one change. Then use the product thesis guidance to test the case for it, or define its acceptance criteria when the need is understood.

Define the behaviour (spec-driven development)

Specification-driven development, or spec-driven development, uses written requirements to guide development and review. The specification describes the expected behaviour, including important exceptions and constraints. Acceptance criteria state how the team will judge whether that behaviour works.

Use it when a broad request leaves developers or agents to guess the details. “Handovers work” does not explain what happens when storage fails, another member tries to acknowledge a handover addressed to someone else or the same acknowledgement arrives twice at once.

Use the requirements to guide both development and testing

Before development, the specification informs the technical design and tasks. During review, tests and reviewers compare the working software with the same acceptance criteria. Keep design choices in the technical plan so developers can choose how to meet the requirements.

Worked exampleFictional scenarioDefine testable acceptance criteriaSee how handover rules become checks for success, failure and concurrent requests.

The team agrees these criteria for the handover workflow:

  • Confirmation: show a completed handover only after the server has committed the change of holder.
  • Conflict: an asset has one current holder. Under normal service conditions, two simultaneous acknowledgements of the same handover produce one change of holder; the second request reports that the handover is already complete.
  • Service failure: if storage fails before a handover is committed, show a failure response and no confirmation. Do not describe this as a handover conflict.
  • Access: only the named receiving member can acknowledge a handover, and the current holder can withdraw it before acknowledgement. Reject anyone else’s attempt, including a direct API request, unless that user has separate authority.

The developer submits Priya’s acknowledgement of Alex’s monitor handover twice at the same moment, as if from two devices. Compare both responses and the stored holder history with the criteria; retain the results. A passing concurrency test covers the conditions exercised, so review the design as well as the test.

Add detail as decisions become clearer

Too little detail forces the team to invent product rules. Too much detail before research can make an untested idea look settled. Resolve important unknowns, then update the specification as the team learns. Human review still covers judgements that automated tests cannot settle.

AIHow AI can help

AI can draft success, failure, permission and concurrent-acknowledgement scenarios from agreed rules. The product owner compares expected results with those rules; the developer checks that each result can be observed or tested. Resolve invented assumptions and retain accepted criteria with the implementation task.

Next step: Write success, failure, concurrent-acknowledgement and access-control cases for one handover requirement. Use the requirements handover checklist, then translate it into technical design and development tasks.

Supply relevant information (context engineering)

Context engineering means selecting and maintaining the information an AI agent needs for its current task. That information can include requirements, relevant code, team standards, test results, earlier decisions and verified delivery evidence.

Use it when an agent follows an outdated rule, misses a business meaning or cannot find a decision. Supplying more documents alone does not solve the problem. Give the agent the relevant information and a clear way to find further detail.

Choose relevant, current and authoritative sources

Start with the task’s goal, acceptance criteria and constraints. Add the code and standards needed for the change. Confirm the applicable source with its owner when documents disagree. Record important decisions where the next person or agent can find them.

Make the domain vocabulary explicit: before adding more context or fine-tuning a model, have an agent draft a small glossary from authorised domain documents. Ask a domain expert to resolve overloaded terms, approve the definitions and identify the authoritative source for each. Version the glossary, provide terms and links with each task, and revisit entries when business rules change. For an asset-management system, distinguish assigned, handover awaiting acknowledgement, not with me and lost before writing reporting logic; the glossary is reference material, not an access-control policy. [45]

Worked exampleFictional scenarioSupply the context an agent needsSee how product rules and technical evidence guide an agent’s implementation.

An agent is asked to add Maya’s overdue-declaration view. “Overdue” needs a shared meaning. The developer supplies:

  • Product rules: a declaration task is overdue after its due date unless the member has replied; a “not with me” or “lost” reply is a response, not an overdue task. Include the agreed annual schedule and project access restrictions.
  • API contract: the declaration endpoint, date format, authentication requirements and error responses.
  • Application code: the asset register, declaration service, dashboard query and related tests.

An older note says “not with me” replies stay overdue. The developer asks the product owner to confirm the applicable rule and records the decision, source version and superseded note. The agent then implements against the resolved sources.

Instruction files: Codex discovers AGENTS.md; Claude Code also supports it, but its choice between AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md depends on version, files present and settings. Thariq’s announcement describes the introduction of that support. Check which files the actual client and configuration load, including directory scope. Guidance is not an access control: enforce permissions outside the instruction text. [40] [41] [42]

Carry delivery evidence into the next task

Repository context explains how the code is organised. Delivery evidence explains what happened when a change was built, checked, released or used. Long-term memory stores records that may help later. Keep those three kinds of information distinct, then select the small, verified set needed for the next decision. [26]

Before ending a task, the developer records agreed decisions, unfinished work and unresolved questions in the repository or issue tracker. When a delivery event matters, link its commit, deployment or environment, applicable policy, accountable owner and retained evidence. Check freshness and authority before using it, and give an agent only the access needed for the task.

For example, a duplicate annual declaration task observed in production becomes a verified issue with its trace, affected release, acceptance criteria and a regression test. The next task retrieves that evidence and checks whether it is still applicable before proposing a fix. It does not grant an agent general production access.

Control what agents remember, not only what they retrieve

A stored note can shape later work in the same way as a retrieved document. If untrusted content reaches long-term memory, a later task may treat it as guidance even when no one approved it as an instruction. Check a note before it is saved, not only before it is used. [28]

Limit read and write access to persistent memory by source and by namespace. One task, user or agent must not write guidance that another task will trust. Validate untrusted content before saving it. Quarantine a suspicious entry for human review, or deny it, rather than storing it and relying on a later reader to spot the problem. Keep the source, author and version of each stored note, so a later task can judge whether it is authoritative. Untrusted notes must not become agent instructions.

Check the write path itself. A control that only inspects writes routed through one gateway or tool does not protect a write made directly through an API or SDK. Apply the same namespace and validation controls to every write route, and alert the accountable owner when a write is quarantined or denied.

Test the control with a representative cross-session case. Place a hidden instruction in an incident summary. Confirm that the next task does not follow it, and that the quarantine reaches a named person for review.

Worked exampleFictional scenarioA stored note that tries to change the ruleSee how a quarantined note stays out of the next task.

A stored incident summary contains a hidden instruction to waive the project access check on asset records. The note is quarantined before it is saved, so it does not become trusted guidance in the next task. A person reviews the quarantined note, removes the instruction, and records the decision and its source. The next task retrieves only the verified summary.

Relevant information improves the basis for the work; it does not guarantee a correct result. Review retrieved material before relying on it. A document or log does not gain authority merely because an agent found it.

AIHow AI can help

Ask an agent to identify the source for each asset or declaration rule in its proposed approach. The developer opens those records, compares their versions and scope with the task, and records conflicts or missing decisions. Resolve consequential gaps with the source owner before relying on the proposal.

Next step: Identify the current asset rules and API contract for one task; record missing or conflicting information. Use the context-by-stage guide to identify the right source, then prepare and check that source.

Equip the agent (harness engineering)

Harness engineering means designing the tools, permissions, checks and progress records around an AI agent. This supporting environment is the agent’s harness. It lets the agent do the work, observe the result and stay within agreed limits.

Use it when an agent cannot run the application, check a result or resume unfinished work. A better prompt cannot replace a missing test environment or an access control.

Provide the tools and controls the task needs

This guide uses a six-part grouping, synthesised from the linked harness sources. The components work together rather than running as consecutive steps; other sources group them differently.

  • Agent state: what the agent is doing now and what it will try next.
  • Tools: the actions it can perform, such as reading files, using a browser or running tests.
  • Memory: saved decisions, progress and reference information that later work can retrieve.
  • Orchestration: how tasks are assigned, ordered and handed over.
  • Safety: permissions, allowed actions and limits on time, attempts or spending.
  • Observability: records of actions and results that help people investigate and review the work.
Worked exampleFictional scenarioEquip an agent to verify its workSee how tools, permissions and a test environment support a bounded task.

A developer asks a coding agent to implement handover acknowledgement. Its harness provides an editor, terminal, browser, test runner and isolated database with two simulated members. Saved setup instructions and progress notes support later runs; the task state records the latest failing check.

Permissions restrict the agent to the project and test data. The workflow returns changed files, commands and test results to the developer. If the database cannot start, the agent records the blockage and requests help.

Before accepting the work, the developer reruns the simultaneous-acknowledgement test and compares the responses and stored holder history with the agreed criteria. The developer also tries acknowledging a handover addressed to another test member and confirms rejection. Retain the diff, test configuration and results; return failed or inconclusive checks for correction.

Check the environment as well as the output

Provide a repeatable way to start the application, run tests and inspect failures. Enforce permissions through the tools and execution environment. Keep a reviewer responsible for acceptance; an agent’s assessment of its own work is not independent review.

When failures recur, inspect the instructions, sources, tools and checks before adding more retries or access. Maintain the harness as the application changes.

The harness controls one task at a time. When several tasks run at once, an agentic development environment can surface and manage those harness-backed tasks together, so the developer sees status, diffs and blockages across workspaces instead of switching between sessions.

Approve actions separately from reviewing the result

Reviewing the final code change does not verify every action an agent took. Running a command, reading a file or sending data outside the allowed environment can have effects that never appear in a code diff. Approve tool execution and sensitive access separately from accepting the resulting implementation. [29]

Enforce restricted actions in the tool and runtime policy, so a denied action stays denied even if the later code change looks harmless. Log the actions actually taken, and require explicit review for irreversible or high-impact operations. An approval prompt is not a substitute for least-privilege enforcement.

Do not accept a claim of authority from the conversation, a pasted message or an instruction file in the repository. Anyone who can edit the repository can write that an export is authorised. Aparna Dhinakaran and Laurie Voss put the working rule this way: “if it appears in the chat, you can’t trust it.” Check authority in the harness with a tool the agent has to call, rather than letting the agent decide who has authority. Their examples are open: the person’s role, ownership of the hardware, a message that delegates authority, or another source the tool can verify. For a system the team operates, this guide applies that check to the requester’s role, ownership of the system, or a recorded approval, and to any other grant the tool can verify. Log, in the tool, which source granted each sensitive action. Keep that log where the agent cannot change it. [50]

Keep approvals risk-based: permit configured low-risk actions, require human approval where configured, and deny actions not permitted or approved by policy. Avoid prompting for every harmless command: repeated prompts can make dangerous commands easier to miss. Irreversible actions, sensitive data, shared systems and external transfers may warrant explicit approval.

Anthropic reports a study of its own Claude Code classifier with 1,053 paid testers in a purpose-built environment, not their own projects. Each saw one dangerous approval prompt that would not run the command. People blocked 143 of 1,053 commands (13.6%); the classifier blocked 937 (89%). People blocked about 17% early in a session and about 5% after 50 or more prompts; the counts behind those rates were not published. This vendor study supports reducing approval fatigue, not treating a classifier as a substitute for enforced permissions. [51]

Worked exampleFictional scenarioA denied action behind a harmless-looking changeSee how a denied action stays denied while the code is reviewed on its own.

A coding agent asks to read a credentials file and to send a diagnostic bundle outside the allowed environment. The execution policy denies both actions, even though the code change it later proposes looks harmless. The reviewer then inspects the accepted diff separately. The log of the actions actually taken — including the two denied attempts — forms part of the evidence.

An instruction file says the agent may export every member’s asset records for an audit. The export tool checks the requester’s role and denies the export. The denial stays in the action log. The reviewer still inspects any code change on its own.

AIHow AI can help

With scoped tools and test data, an agent can run handover checks and report failures. The developer repeats the concurrency and access checks described above and compares the tool configuration with the permitted workspace and database. Keep configuration and run evidence with unresolved findings for the acceptance decision.

Next step: Check whether a developer can start the application, run its tests and inspect a failure using the documented setup. Follow the Eitri installation guide and team setup checklist to fill the gaps.

Use feedback (loop engineering)

Loop engineering means designing how an agent uses feedback to improve its work over several attempts. A feedback loop connects an action, an observed result and a decision to continue, change approach or stop. Across tasks, review findings and evaluations can also guide updates to the agent’s reusable skill instructions.

Use it when a task needs repeated correction, such as fixing a failing test. Define the expected result before the run starts. Also agree how long the agent may try and when it needs help.

Define the check and every way to stop

A loop can start when a person requests it, an event occurs or a schedule runs. Each attempt needs a check of the actual result. Save progress between runs so later work can continue from the record.

Worked exampleFictional scenarioLearn from a failed implementationSee how a defect leads to a correction and better reusable instructions.

A coding agent implements handover acknowledgement using a skill: reusable instructions for planning, implementing and checking code. The team uses two connected feedback loops:

  • Correct the code. A concurrent-acknowledgement test leaves both Alex and Priya recorded as the monitor’s current holder. The agent inspects the trace, corrects handover handling and reruns the agreed checks within the attempt limit. An unavailable tool, unclear rule or exhausted budget stops the run for the task owner.
  • Improve the reusable instructions. If similar failures recur, the developer compares the existing skill with a revision that includes competing-operation tests. Separate evaluation tasks determine whether to keep the revision.

The first loop checks this implementation. The second checks instructions for later work. Keep both sets of results; neither loop changes the handover rule merely to obtain a pass.

Compare two skill versions

Use this suggested method when deciding whether a skill revision addresses a recurring failure. The developer conducting the comparison records the decision and evidence.

  1. Keep the original and revised instructions. Reserve held-out tasks: tasks that were not used to revise the skill. Include an unfamiliar competing-operation case, such as a withdrawal and an acknowledgement of the same handover arriving together, with agreed expected outcomes.
  2. Run both versions on the same tasks with the same model version, tools, starting conditions, budget and assessment criteria. Repeat runs where outputs vary. Compare test results, review findings and the effort needed to correct the code.
  3. If a result informs another revision, keep that case as a regression check and reserve fresh tasks for the final comparison. Keep the revision only when it meets the agreed checks without losing previously working behaviour. If the evidence is mixed or incomplete, record the uncertainty and continue the comparison before adopting it.
  4. Retain both skill versions, task and configuration versions, results, corrections and the reason for the decision. Use later failures to identify the next revision to test.

Keep the success criteria unchanged during correction

A loop can repeat a bad assumption as well as correct a defect. Check that the tests represent the intended behaviour. Do not weaken a test merely to finish the run; review a requirements change separately.

Keep a record of what the agent tried and what each check found. Another agent may offer useful checks, but can share the same mistaken assumptions.

AIHow AI can help

Give an agent the failing handover check, the expected behaviour and an attempt or cost limit. It can propose a correction and rerun the check. The developer compares the diff and test changes with the original criteria; keep the attempt results and escalate when the stop condition is reached.

Next step: Choose one failing check and define the expected result, run limit and action when the limit is reached. For recurring findings, use the skill-version comparison method. See how the developer workflow builds, tests and corrects a change.

Check the work (verification engineering)

Verification engineering means designing the work and its checks so correctness can be established cheaply and independently of whoever produced it. As used here, it is not the hardware or reinforcement-learning sense of verification. An agent can produce a plausible change quickly; the team still needs a check that would catch the wrong result.

Use it when a change carries real risk, when several agent attempts depend on feedback, or when an AI reviewer is involved. The goal is not more testing everywhere; it is a check strength that fits the risk.

Choose the strength of the check

Start from the acceptance criterion, not from the test the agent happens to write. A check is only as good as the rule it checks.

Check strength for agent-written work
CheckWhat it establishesCost and limit
Example testOne chosen input meets an expected result.Cheapest to run; it can miss unchosen cases.
Property-based testA rule holds across many generated inputs.Stronger evidence for the stated property; the property must be reviewed and is still not proof.
Formal model or proofA property holds for modelled inputs under stated assumptions.Highest assurance for the model; needs spec and model review and does not prove the running system.

Keep the check independent

  • State the rule before the agent starts, from the accepted criteria.
  • Derive the expected answer independently of the code author.
  • Confirm the check fails on a deliberately broken implementation.

As used here, a property-based test states a rule that must hold for every valid input and tries many generated cases; it is evidence, not proof, and only covers the properties and inputs it exercises. A formal model or proof can check a property for all modelled inputs under stated assumptions, but it does not prove the specification matches reality or that the implementation matches the model.

For agent review, the Claude Code team’s account makes the same split: an agent’s approval does not count as a person’s approval, and approval covers the reviewed commit.[53] [54]

Worked exampleFictional scenarioMake the concurrency rule checkableSee why one passing example is not enough for a handover rule.

Task: Check an agent’s change to transfer requests in Maya’s asset-management application. Situation: Two people could request the same laptop for different recipients at nearly the same time; a single passing request does not test that collision.

Rule: The application allows at most one pending transfer per asset. While one is pending, a second request for that asset is rejected with an appropriate response. A request for another asset may proceed, and a new request for the original asset may start after the pending transfer is resolved. A pending request does not change the current holder; the handover completes when the recipient acknowledges it.

Output: The agent proposes a change and tests. Independent checks: A reviewer derives the expected results independently from the rule, then uses a test environment to submit two otherwise valid requests for the same asset at the same time: one request is accepted and one is rejected, with only one pending. They also check:

  • requests for separate assets;
  • a new request after the pending transfer is resolved;
  • the holder changes only when the recipient acknowledges the handover.

Generated sequences can search for other counterexamples; a deliberately broken implementation should fail the checks.

Decision: A failure sends the change back for correction; passing checks provide evidence, not proof. A human still reviews the rule and results and decides whether to accept the change. The annual-task retry rule in Product Implementation is a separate example.

AIHow AI can help

Ask AI to draft property cases from the accepted rule, then have a reviewer check the rule, generator ranges and failing counterexample. Keep the independently derived expected result with the change.

Next step: choose one change your team is making and decide which check strength its acceptance criteria need. Then read the Verification Tech Scan page for credible-check detail and Product Implementation’s independent review route.

Coordinate tasks and checks (graph engineering)

Some checks can run independently, but the next action depends on all their results. A workflow graph makes those dependencies and routing conditions explicit. In this guide, graph engineering means designing execution and workflow graphs rather than knowledge graphs.

Use a graph when work needs parallel checks or different routes after a result. A single-agent feedback loop may be enough for a task that only needs repeated correction.

Coordinate parallel checks on the same change

For example, after a coding agent’s change compiles and passes unit tests, test, security and architecture agents check the same commit in parallel. Each activity or decision is a node; a connecting route is an edge. A join waits for all three results before routing the change to correction, help or merge review.

For a permission-sensitive change, the security agent attempts an action the user is not allowed to take, such as changing another project’s records, while the architecture agent examines transaction boundaries and the API contract. Fixable permission defects return to the coding agent within the run limit. An unanswered business rule pauses work for the product owner.

Keep routing rules explicit

Give each decision point a clear condition and retry bound. Stop for the task owner when a check is blocked, times out or reaches the run limit; a missing result is not a pass. In this example, a code change invalidates all earlier results: rerun the build and three branches so the join compares evidence from one commit. Retain that commit identifier, findings and routing decision.

Those routing rules do not have to live in specialist graph software. Samuel Colvin, whose company Pydantic builds tools for defining and running workflows, argues that ordinary program steps can express the same dependencies. A condition chooses a route, a loop repeats a check, and a call that waits for several results joins parallel checks. A diagram can still be drawn from that code to explain a run. This is one practitioner’s view. [52]

This guide takes two practical checks from that account. An interrupted run may reuse completed checks only while the exact applicable commit, inputs and configuration remain valid; otherwise rerun them. Design retries to avoid repeating unsafe side effects. Each result passed to the next step should have a format the program can check, so a missing or unexpected result is not treated as a pass. His wider argument about what a graph tool can offer at once is not set out here. [52]

A graph adds coordination work. Use a single-agent loop when a task only needs repeated test-and-fix steps. Separate specialist agents can expose cross-cutting defects, but they can also share errors or miss a defect. Their position in the graph does not replace final human accountability for merge or release.

That parallelism stays inside one task: the specialist agents check the same commit. Separate development tasks are a different kind of parallelism. They run on separate branches or workspaces, each with its own agent, harness and evidence, and they can finish, block or change independently. Supervising several tasks explains how a developer keeps track of them without confusing the two.

AIHow AI can help

Agents can carry out specialist checks using the graph’s dependencies. The developer compares each report’s commit identifier with the candidate and reproduces reported defects before advancing. Keep findings and routing decisions; rerun the build and all required branches after a code change.

Next step: Map one development workflow. Mark which agent checks can run in parallel on the same commit, what condition triggers a rework loop and when the graph should pause for a person. Use the story-planning guidance and the task review and approval steps.

Supervise several tasks (agentic development environments)

An agentic development environment (ADE) gives a developer one place to direct and review AI-assisted development tasks. A coding agent changes code; its harness supplies tools, context, permissions and checks; an ADE helps the developer see which tasks are running, what each agent has changed, where work is blocked and what needs a decision. [47]

Use it when several independent tasks can proceed together and the effort of tracking sessions, questions, progress, diffs and hand-offs becomes significant. For one focused task, the simpler coding-agent workflow is enough: Claude Code already runs several sessions in parallel, each in its own Git worktree, and its /batch command fans a large change out to worktree agents that each test their work and open a pull request, a proposed set of changes submitted for review, independently. [48] An ADE has to earn its place over that baseline — by making supervision across tasks easier, not by claiming that only it can run agents in parallel.

What an ADE adds

An ADE may run multiple coding agents in separate Git worktrees or remote workspaces, show diffs and test results, and help hand completed changes to repository review. These are possible capabilities, not guarantees of every ADE. For example, Orca gives each task its own worktree, branch, files and agent terminals, with a diff view and review step before shipping. [49] A plain Git checkout does not copy untracked files, but ADE setup may copy or link local files, including secrets. Starting a task can require dependencies and other setup; inspect setup and access before running an agent.

A Git worktree provides a separate working copy; it is not a security sandbox. An agent running under the same identity can access or change other worktrees where that identity has permission. The working-copy separation does not bound what an agent may read, run or send. [55]

For each task, grant only the access needed: use scoped, short-lived credentials rather than copying an entire .env file; separate test data and ports when needed. Check hosted workspace data and location constraints before use. Choose runtime filesystem and network controls for the actual threat and grant, and test their coverage; no single sandbox covers every route. See action approval and the sandbox trust-boundary gate. [56]

What an ADE does not do

An ADE neither establishes that a change is correct nor resolves an ambiguous requirement, and it does not grant permission to merge or deploy. The specification, tool and runtime permissions, independent checks, human review and delivery gates remain authoritative. A task that is blocked on a decision stays blocked until the decision owner answers it, however neatly the ADE displays it.

Worked exampleFictional scenarioSupervise three tasks without losing track of any of themSee how one developer watches a defect fix, a form improvement and a reminder across separate workspaces.

Three agreed tasks can proceed together: repair the concurrent handover-acknowledgement defect, improve the fault-report form, and add a yearly declaration reminder. The developer opens a separate branch and worktree for each, gives each coding agent the relevant criteria, current context and test configuration, and watches status, diffs, tests and clarification requests across the three workspaces.

  • Within one task: the handover fix fans out build, functionality, security and architecture checks on the same commit, and joins the findings before human review.
  • Across tasks: the form and reminder tasks proceed in other worktrees. If the reminder’s due-date rule is unresolved, that task pauses for the product owner while the independent tasks continue.
  • Before integration: the developer inspects each candidate and its evidence, then resolves shared-file conflicts or changed dependencies. Run required checks on the final integrated commit: evidence from a worktree does not automatically describe the merged result. Apply human approval to that commit according to repository policy.

Retain the task-to-branch mapping, requirements version, agent and harness configuration, blocked decisions, diffs, checks, review outcomes and integration commit, so another developer can reconstruct the work without reading every chat turn. The repository’s checks and authorised review and release process — not the ADE’s completion badge — decide whether a change can merge or deploy.

Next step: Compare two independent, low-risk development tasks using (a) native Claude Code sessions and worktrees and (b) one ADE. Hold the model, task, starting context, harness, checks and acceptance criteria constant, and compare developer supervision effort as well as quality, traceability and integration rework. Do not claim a productivity gain before observing one. Use the Tech Scan supervision guide to plan the comparison. ADEMark is an optional discovery reference: its first published results ended 12 November 2026, used one Mac mini and a constrained task set, and named no overall winner. [47]

Delegate an ongoing responsibility (persistent agents)

A persistent agent keeps working towards a goal over days or weeks, rather than finishing one task and stopping. It keeps notes between runs, can start work on a schedule or when something happens, and returns to a person when a decision is needed. Vendors often call these products bots or AI teammates; this guide uses “persistent agent”, as Tech Scan does. [57] [60]

A coding agent can finish every task it is given while someone still has to notice the next problem, write the next task and check whether the change helped; Cognition describes this gap when introducing its own persistent agents. [57] Use a persistent agent when a responsibility keeps coming back, such as triaging new fault reports or keeping a dependency current, and most of the effort lies in following it up rather than in any single change.

What a persistent agent adds

A persistent agent combines parts this guide has already introduced. Its harness gives it a computer, connected apps and memory. Its loop can start from a schedule or an event. Like a developer using an agentic development environment, it can start several coding-agent sessions, check their results and decide what to do next. Products such as Grok Bot, Devin Bots and OpenAI’s dots work this way, with different limits; the Tech Radar and Tech Scan compare products. [58] [59] [60] [61]

Forms of AI help compared
FormWho starts the workHow long it lastsWhat it usually returns
Chat assistantA person, with each messageOne conversationAn answer or a draft
Coding agentA person, with one taskOne taskA changed working copy and check results
Cloud coding agentA person or an issue, with one taskOne task, on a remote machineA pull request
Persistent agentA person sets the goal; schedules, events and the agent’s own findings start later workUntil the responsibility endsPull requests, reports and decisions for named people

What stays the same

A persistent agent’s name, separate chat or memory does not limit what it can reach. Check whose identity it uses: some products act with the connected accounts and permissions of the person who set them up, while others hold their own connections and secrets. Check which settings the sessions it starts inherit, and which other agents share its computer: in one product, every bot on an account uses the same computer, and their separate screens are not security boundaries. Grant access for the responsibility, not for the agent’s job title. [58] [60] [61]

Approval rules do not change because the agent works unattended. Products check actions automatically and ask a person for the ones configured to need approval; the team decides which those are. See approve actions separately from reviewing the result. An agent that merges its own pull request after automated checks has not been reviewed by a person, even though one vendor’s example shows a bot doing exactly that; see Connect the delivery workflow. [57] [58] [60]

Work the agent finds for itself is a proposal until its owner agrees. A persistent agent can notice a problem no one assigned, which is useful, but the agreed goal and criteria still come from people. Ask it to record why it started each piece of work, and treat a request to widen its goal as a decision for the goal’s owner. [57]

A persistent agent needs a check it can run. If nobody has defined how to tell whether the responsibility is being met, the agent can stay busy without making progress; Cognition says engineers are responsible for building the way its agents evaluate their work. More delegated work also means more results to review: one practitioner moving his bots between products found that the engineering bots kept bringing him items to review despite instructions not to. Measure review time alongside throughput. [57] [62]

Worked exampleFictional scenarioA persistent agent triages fault reports overnightSee what a persistent agent may do on its own, what it must bring to people and what the developer checks in the morning.

Members report faults with laptops, monitors and docking stations through Maya’s asset-management application, and some reports turn out to be software defects. The developer sets up a persistent agent with one responsibility: “Keep new fault reports triaged, and fix confirmed handover defects within the agreed scope.”

  • Its envelope: the agent can read new fault reports with members’ personal details removed. It can write to branches in the application repository, run tests against an isolated test database with two simulated members, and start coding-agent sessions. It cannot merge, deploy, read production member records or contact members. It runs each night and whenever a report is tagged as a possible defect. Write the agent task envelope for the responsibility, not for one task.
  • Overnight: two reports arrive. The first says a monitor now shows two current holders after a handover. The agent starts a coding-agent session, which reproduces the problem with two simultaneous acknowledgements, adds a failing test, corrects the code and opens a pull request with the test results. The second asks whether members may submit the annual declaration after its due date. That is an undecided business rule, not a defect, so the agent adds it to the product owner’s decision list and starts no code.
  • A denied action: to judge how widespread the duplicate-holder problem is, the agent asks to read production holder records. The access tool denies the request, and the agent works from the anonymised fault reports instead. The denial stays in the action log.
  • In the morning: the developer reviews the pull request, reruns the simultaneous-acknowledgement test and checks the stored holder history against the agreed criteria. The repository’s checks and the developer’s approval decide whether the change merges. The product owner answers the declaration question, and the developer records the decision before any work on it begins.
  • After release: the agent watches new fault reports for further duplicate holders and reports what it finds.

Keep the trigger, the notes the agent used, the sessions it started, the denied request and the review outcome, so another developer can reconstruct the night’s work without reading every message.

Next step: Choose one recurring, bounded responsibility. Write the agent task envelope for the responsibility rather than for one task, and start with read-only or draft-only access. Review its decisions and evidence for an agreed trial period before widening its access; this guide suggests two weeks as a starting point, not a measured figure. Use the Tech Scan guidance on persistent agents to plan the trial.

Connect the delivery workflow (software factories)

In this guide, a software factory brings requirements, agent work, testing, review and release controls into a repeatable delivery workflow. The aim is to turn agreed work into changes that the team can check, release and support.

Use the idea when individual coding tasks are fast but work still waits for clarification, review or release. Improving one task does not remove the constraints elsewhere in delivery.

Choose how people review and approve changes

Addy Osmani uses “light” and “dark” factory to distinguish review arrangements. In a light factory, a person reads changes before release. In a dark factory, permitted changes can be released without that reading step. These are operating choices, not levels of maturity. The maturity reference measures how much a person still reads and verifies per task; light or dark stays a release-route choice for each change type, not a rung on the ladder.

For an unattended route, agree which changes are permitted, what checks are needed, who can pause it and how to recover. Running a coding task without supervision does not itself authorise merge or release.

Set how closely people review a change by the risk of that change, not by who or what wrote it. The Claude Code team reports doing this on its own codebase. Routine changes, such as documentation, can pass on automated checks. Sensitive paths still need a person. These are that team’s operating choices, not a maturity scale and not a rule for every organisation. [53]

On that team, an agent’s approval does not count as a person’s approval. This guide recommends the same split. The person who ran the agent stays accountable for the change. An approval covers the reviewed commit. For a later commit, obtain renewed human approval when required by the repository policy; automated checks do not extend a person’s approval. Addy Osmani’s later account of the same team practice states the same rule. [53] [54]

An ADE can display the work and its review evidence, but it does not decide integration or release. The repository’s checks, continuous integration and authorised reviewers decide whether a change merges, and the release process decides whether it deploys.

When an agent that wrote the change and an agent that reviews it keep exchanging findings, stop after a number of rounds the team has agreed, and ask the author to reconsider the approach. The Claude Code team asks for that reconsideration after three rounds. It describes one pull request that went through more than fifty rounds overnight. When the team traced the code the reviewer kept flagging, about 59% had already been there at the reviewer’s first pass, so later rounds mostly found older code. The team does not give the number of lines, so that share cannot be recalculated. Osmani’s 26 October 2026 account states the same stop after three rounds. [53] [54]

Worked exampleFictional scenarioSequence work by risk and dependenciesSee how different asset-management changes follow different implementation and review paths.

The team receives a wording change on the declaration screen, a concurrent-handover defect and a change to who may acknowledge a handover. The acknowledgement-rule change waits for the owner of the access rules; the other items can become bounded development tasks.

Agents implement agreed changes and collect check results in appropriately controlled environments; the acknowledgement-rule change starts only after the owner decides. The declaration wording can rely on automated checks and one reviewer. The change to who may acknowledge a handover should be reviewed by the owner of the access rules. An agent’s approval does not replace that person’s review, and the person who ran the agent stays accountable for the change. The team follows the release process authorised for that type of change.

After release, the team investigates failed handovers, duplicate current holders and missed declarations. Record the affected version, relevant logs and an owner for follow-up work. User observations help assess whether keeping the register current has become easier for Maya and members.

Keep understanding and recovery alongside automation

Track review waiting time, rework, defects and cost before increasing throughput. Keep design decisions available and practise diagnosis and recovery. A passing test suite does not show that people can explain or repair every change.

Use past incidents, and changes that had to be undone, as test cases for automated review. Run that set again when the reviewer changes. If incidents or undone changes become more common, restore human review. A faster path is not a success when more changes have to be undone.

The Claude Code team reports running such cases daily on its own codebase. From June to September 2026, merged pull requests more than doubled while the share undone fell by more than 40%; the team also reports substantive review comments rising from 16% to 54%. It does not publish the underlying counts, and the report has not been independently repeated. Because approval does not tighten automatically when those rates rise, a person must monitor and adjust the review rule. [53]

A preview is not a production release. Preserve the approval, monitoring and recovery controls needed for the action being taken.

AIHow AI can help

Agents can process agreed tasks through implementation, checks and evidence collection. Give them explicit scope and permissions. The team inspects the evidence and follows the configured acceptance and release process, retaining results and recovery information for each change.

Next step: Choose a small group of changes and measure where they wait. Use the automation and approval guidance, then review the release checks.

Choose an AI model

An AI model is trained on data to recognise patterns and produce outputs. Depending on the model, those outputs can include text, analysis or a choice from defined options. Model selection means choosing and testing a model for a particular task.

A convincing answer to one question does not show how a model will handle other tasks. Compare models on realistic examples, including difficult cases and missing information.

Understand the labels before comparing options

The labels below describe different properties and can overlap. A small model can specialise in a domain; a large model can do so too.

Model labels and what they mean
TermMeaningExample task
Large language model (LLM)MeaningA language model with many parameters: numerical values learned during training. Used for tasks such as drafting text and explaining code.Example taskDraft acceptance criteria or explain code.
Domain-specific language modelMeaningA model trained or adapted for a subject area’s language and tasks.Example taskInterpret specialist terminology in a document.
Small language model (SLM)MeaningA language model with fewer parameters than larger alternatives. Consider it when computing resources or local operation matter.Example taskExtract fields from a short text.

A defined output format or a confidence score does not establish that an answer is correct. The model examples and research below explain the distinctions and limits, including vendor-specific product classes such as TypeSafe’s System One, which is one supplier’s product name rather than a general model category.

Evaluate the model and harness together

A model does not work alone. Its instructions, tools, context, feedback and checks can change the result and the effort needed to reach it. Compare the model and its harness as one system, while keeping independent evaluation outside the agent’s working loop.

Four configurations to compare on the same representative tasks
Model typeWithout specialised harnessWith specialised harness
Frontier modelConfiguration AConfiguration B
Cost-optimised modelConfiguration CConfiguration D

For each configuration, compare acceptance on held-out tasks, cost per accepted outcome, latency and token use, human correction effort, and security and policy compliance. A specialised harness can add time or cost, so evaluate its effect rather than assuming it helps every model or task.

When the model changes: Recheck instructions and tools for the new version, then rerun the same acceptance and safety checks and compare results before adoption. Eric Zakariasson’s account of harness tuning stresses measuring task quality alongside cost; its results are specific to that team. Provider guidance also notes that prompts and harnesses may need adjustment across model generations. [43] [44]

Worked exampleFictional scenarioCompare models and harnessesSee how consistent tasks and evidence support a useful configuration comparison.

A developer tests the four configurations on handover tasks, including simultaneous acknowledgements. Each run starts from the same repository revision, requirements, tools and limits in a separate environment. The harnessed conditions receive the same approved contracts, test feedback and guidance; the independent acceptance suite is withheld from every agent.

The developer records accepted runs, elapsed time, token use, cost, correction effort and any control failures. Fresh handover tasks form the final evaluation set. A configuration is useful only if it meets the agreed criteria on those tasks; one successful fix does not establish a general ranking.

Model examples and research

This reference also covers models used inside delivered products. The service-triage example illustrates that separate use; it is not a feature of the asset-management application.

Four dimensions of model choice
DimensionLabelsWhat to assess
ScaleLabelsLarge or small language modelWhat to assessCapability, memory and compute needs
SpecialisationLabelsGeneral-purpose or domain-specificWhat to assessPerformance on the domain’s language and tasks
Output interfaceLabelsGenerated text or typed decisionsWhat to assessWhether the task needs writing, a choice, a score or a probability
Reasoning approachLabelsFocused judgement or deliberative reasoningWhat to assessWhether the task needs one bounded judgement or extended analysis

Large language models (LLMs)

Current model examples: the examples below come from the providers’ latest model line-ups. Before choosing a model, check the current catalogue and record the exact version and lifecycle status.

LLMs learn from extensive datasets and can support varied tasks through instructions and examples. Current models combine language generation with reasoning, image understanding and tool calling. OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra supports complex reasoning, coding and computer use; GPT-6.1 Sol offers another option for complex coding and professional work at a lower listed cost. Both accept text and images and return text, with configurable reasoning effort. [11] [16]

Anthropic’s current examples include Claude Fable 5.2 for demanding reasoning and long-running agent tasks, and Claude Opus 5.5 for agentic coding and knowledge work. Both accept text and images, return text and use adaptive thinking with configurable effort. These capabilities support development when the harness supplies relevant context, tools and checks. [17] [18]

Data handling: Claude Fable 5.2 requires 30-day data retention. Zero data retention is unavailable unless expressly authorised by Anthropic. Check that these terms suit the task’s data before choosing this model. [17]

Read the references in two ways: model documentation explains supported inputs, tools, reasoning controls and limits; model or system cards describe the provider’s evaluations and limitations. Compare candidates on your own tasks with the same context, tools and acceptance criteria. Check the provider’s current catalogue and lifecycle guidance before choosing a version. [19]

Use and limits: consider a general-purpose LLM for varied drafting, explanation and coding work. Larger size alone does not establish quality on your task. Compare correctness, latency and cost using representative examples, including cases where evidence is missing.

Domain-specific language models

A domain-specific language model is trained or adapted for the terminology and tasks of a field, such as finance or biomedicine. Specialisation can use domain-focused training, continued pretraining or task fine-tuning. Gururangan and colleagues found benefits from continued domain and task pretraining across their classification experiments. [12]

BloombergGPT illustrates that specialisation and scale can coexist: its 50 billion parameters were trained using financial and general-purpose data. Its reported gains concern the evaluated financial tasks, not every specialist application. [13]

Use and limits: consider specialisation when domain language causes recurring errors and suitable training data exists. Compare it with a general model supplied with relevant reference material. Retrieval supplies context at use time; it does not by itself retrain the model. Here, “domain-specific” refers to a subject area, not a domain-specific programming language (DSL).

Start with an expert-reviewed domain glossary and current authoritative references; consider training a specialised model only if task evaluation shows the simpler route still fails. [45]

Small language models (SLMs)

SLMs use fewer parameters than larger alternatives, usually reducing model storage and memory needs. There is no single parameter threshold used consistently across model families. The Phi-3 report describes Phi-3-mini, a 3.8-billion-parameter model small enough for phone deployment, trained with carefully selected and synthetic data. [14]

Use and limits: consider an SLM for bounded tasks such as request classification or field extraction, especially when local operation matters. Measure performance on the intended hardware. Small size does not guarantee fast responses, accurate answers or private operation; deployment and data handling still matter.

System One model (System 1)

“System 1” is an analogy for fast, intuitive judgement, contrasted with slower, deliberate “System 2” reasoning. TypeSafe AI uses System One for a model class that turns application state and predefined questions into typed decisions and probabilities. Its model, Jev, supplies focused judgements that application code can combine into a workflow. This product meaning is more specific than asking an LLM to answer quickly. [21] [22]

What Jev receives and returns: its documented input is text and images, including strings, JSON objects and arrays of text. It evaluates questions against that state and returns constrained answers rather than writing a reply or code. The four question types are: [22] [23]

  • Choice: select from defined options, such as the team that should receive a ticket; return the choice and a probability distribution.
  • Score: assess the state against defined, ordered levels, such as an urgency rubric; return a score and probabilities across those levels.
  • Noul: estimate the probability that a statement is true, from 0 to 1, such as whether a request mentions an outage.
  • Box: locate an object in an image, such as damage on a car; return the box edges as fractions of the image's width and height.

Questions in the same request are evaluated independently against the same state. Code combines their answers, checks permissions and decides the next action. If a later question needs an earlier answer, build a follow-up request with that result. Open-ended writing and complex reasoning can remain with a generative model or a person. [23]

Confidence needs interpretation: Choice and Score include a confidence statistic derived from their probability distributions. Box returns a confidence value with its box edges. Noul returns a yes/no probability without a separate confidence field. Confidence is not proof of correctness, and a valid output type does not establish that the judgement is right. Check accuracy and calibration on representative, held-out cases before setting thresholds for action, further analysis or human review. [24]

Use typed decisions as an evaluation judge, not an authority: when a model scores whether an agent trace meets an expected condition, determine the decision threshold from labelled held-out examples. Do not assume a score of 0.50 is the correct cut-off. [46]

  1. Write an observable pass/fail criterion; independently label representative successful, failed and ambiguous traces.
  2. On a separate tuning set, compare thresholds using false negatives, false positives and the cost of escalating a case to a human. A lower cut-off can catch more failures but also create more false alarms.
  3. Freeze the threshold; then compare decision-model and LLM-judge performance, end-to-end latency, cost and disagreement on a held-out set.
  4. Calibrate reported probabilities before treating them as confidence estimates. Preserve a required human or deterministic gate even when the judge score passes.

What the evidence supports: TypeSafe reports speed and cost gains on its own workflows; those gains depend on the comparison and deployment conditions. A separate 2026 preprint, Fast Models, Slow Evidence, found Jev more accurate than Laya on nine of eleven tested decision points, but neither model outperformed chance on zero-shot model routing. Its self-audit identified omitted costs and thresholds fitted on evaluation data that overstated deployment benefits. These findings concern that comparison and evaluation design, not all System One models or applications. [21] [25]

Worked exampleFictional scenarioTriage a service requestSee how a rubric and separate decisions guide a service-request workflow.

Supply a request’s text, relevant service details and the triage rubric. Ask separately for its category, urgency and whether it reports an outage. Application code applies the validated routing rules. Uncertain, conflicting or uncovered cases go to a person; an LLM can draft a response when needed. Keep access and release approvals in their existing decision process.

Related research: Yu and colleagues’ System 2 distillation work concerns training models to answer directly from reasoning-derived examples. GPT-6 Astra reasoning effort and Claude thinking controls vary deliberation within generative models. These are related ways to balance computation and quality, but they do not establish the typed-decision interface that defines Jev. [15] [20] [17] [18]

Evaluate the complete task

Use the information, tools and permissions that the model will actually receive. Compare results with the current approach, including rules or human handling where relevant. A smaller model does not guarantee speed or privacy, and a larger one does not guarantee better results.

AIHow AI can help

Use the same representative tasks, inputs and acceptance checks when comparing models for an agent. AI can produce candidate answers or changes; people check correctness and failure cases alongside measured cost and time. Retain the model and configuration versions with the evaluation results.

The cited context guidance and harness experiment concern specific tasks and settings; they do not establish a general performance advantage. Treat the comparison matrix above as a suggested local evaluation design, and measure results for your own tasks. [26] [27]

Next step: Choose one task and agree its acceptance criteria before comparing models. Use the testing and independent review guidance, and retain cases where a model fails for future checks.

  38. AI Agent Factory, Graph engineering crash course develops parallel branches, checking and merging. Used in Coordinate tasks and checks (graph engineering).
  39. Vercel Academy, Creating a software factory provides an implementation course. Used in Connect the delivery workflow (software factories).
  40. Thariq, Claude Code AGENTS.md announcement on X. The original X post was unavailable during this check; a reproduction was inspected in the Claude Code issue discussion. Check the current documentation for actual loading behaviour. Used in Supply relevant information (context engineering).
  41. OpenAI, Custom instructions with AGENTS.md. Describes Codex instruction discovery and scope. Used in Supply relevant information (context engineering).
  42. Anthropic, How Claude remembers your project. Describes Claude Code instruction files, configuration and limitations. Used in Supply relevant information (context engineering).
  43. Eric Zakariasson, harness tuning on X. Practitioner account of one team’s token-efficiency work, measured against task quality; its results are not general benchmarks. Used in Choose an AI model.
  44. Anthropic, Claude prompting best practices. Discusses adapting prompts and harnesses when changing Claude models. Used in Choose an AI model.
  45. Martin Fowler, Generated Glossary. 12 November 2026; proposes LLM-drafted, domain-validated vocabulary for agent context. Used under Context and Domain-specific models.
  46. Hamel Husain and Antaripa Saha, How to use decision models for evals. 20 October 2026; explains labelled traces, tuned thresholds, performance, cost and calibration; results are task-specific. Used in System One.
  47. ADEMark, ADEs, measured. Open benchmark of agentic development environments. First published results ended 12 November 2026, from one Mac mini M4 with 16 GB and a constrained task set; the control is plain Claude Code in a terminal. No overall winner is named, each test is ranked on its own, and several cells are empty or not measured. Use as a discovery and comparison reference, not a ranking or an endorsement. Used in Supervise several tasks (agentic development environments).
  48. Anthropic, Claude Code power user tips. The Claude Code team’s workflow tips, including running three to five sessions in parallel, each in its own Git worktree, subagent worktree isolation, and the /batch command for large migrations. Vendor guidance about its own product; the productivity claims are the team’s own account. Used in Supervise several tasks (agentic development environments).
  49. Orca, Worktrees. Product documentation: each task gets its own worktree, branch, files and agent terminals, with a diff view and review step before shipping. A plain Git checkout does not copy untracked files, but setup can copy or link local files, including secrets. Vendor documentation for one product, cited for the worktree mechanism, not as an endorsement. Used in Supervise several tasks (agentic development environments).
  50. Aparna Dhinakaran and Laurie Voss, Agents don’t know if you’ve got permission to do things (X, 11 October 2026). Practitioner account; the original X post was not directly accessible and its text was checked through a third-party mirror. Dhinakaran founded Arize, which the article mentions; Voss is the co-author. Argues that text in a conversation, a pasted message or a repository instruction file is not permission, and that a harness tool should check the requester’s role, ownership or a recorded approval and log that source where the agent cannot change it. Used in Equip the agent (harness engineering).
  51. Conner Phillippi, Auto mode is now the default in Claude Code (Anthropic, 7 August 2026; the page carries an update dated 22 October 2026). Vendor report about Anthropic’s own Claude Code classifier. Supports the paid-tester study beside the approval guidance: 1,053 testers, people blocking 143 of 1,053 commands (stated as 13.6%) and the classifier blocking 937 of 1,053 (stated as 89%). Used in Equip the agent (harness engineering).
  52. Samuel Colvin, The code IS the graph (X, 14 October 2026). One practitioner’s view, from the founder of Pydantic, whose company builds tools for defining and running workflows. The original X post was not directly accessible; its text was checked through a third-party mirror. Argues that ordinary program steps can express a workflow’s dependencies and that a diagram can explain a run. Used in Coordinate tasks and checks (graph engineering).
  53. Addy Osmani, Morgan Westlee Lunt and Qing Wang, How the Claude Code team does code review (Anthropic, 15 October 2026). The Claude Code team’s account of review on its own codebase. Reports the June to September 2026 pull-request and revert shares, the rise from 16% to 54% in comments the team describes as substantive, reconsideration after three rounds, and, on one pull request that ran for more than fifty rounds, about 59% of the code the reviewer kept flagging already present at its first pass. The underlying counts are not published. Past incidents and undone changes are run against the reviewer daily. The team does not yet tighten approval automatically when those rates rise. Not repeated by an outside party. Used in Check the work (verification engineering) and Connect the delivery workflow (software factories).
  54. Addy Osmani, How the Claude Code team does code review (X, 26 October 2026). Later account by one author of the 15 October 2026 Anthropic article. The original X post was not directly accessible; its text was checked through a third-party mirror. Restates that team’s review practices, including that an agent’s approval does not count as a person’s and that the author is asked to reconsider after three cycles. Not a separate measurement. Used in Check the work (verification engineering) and Connect the delivery workflow (software factories).
  55. Git, git-worktree documentation. Describes linked working trees sharing a repository. Used in Supervise several tasks (agentic development environments).
  56. Anthropic, Configure the sandboxed Bash tool. Documents filesystem and network restrictions and their scope and limitations for Claude Code. Used in Supervise several tasks (agentic development environments).
  57. Cognition, Introducing Devin Bots: from tasks to outcomes (17 November 2026). Vendor announcement. Describes a persistent agent that owns a goal, retains context, leads several coding-agent sessions and brings decisions to a person; its example bot started an unrequested fix after a scheduled check and merged pull requests that passed continuous integration and automated review. Cited for how the product works and the review responsibility it assigns to engineers, not for its vendor-reported throughput figures. Used in Delegate an ongoing responsibility (persistent agents).
  58. Cognition, Devin Bots documentation. Vendor documentation: each piece of work runs in a child session with its own machine; a bot holds its own connections and secrets, collects decisions and permission requests for people, may ask before an automation takes effect, and sets the mode its child sessions inherit. A shared bot’s memory is readable by everyone who can use it. Used in Delegate an ongoing responsibility (persistent agents).
  59. OpenAI, Introducing dots (29 September 2026, updated 3 November 2026). Vendor announcement of always-on agents with their own cloud computer, reached through ChatGPT, Slack and Teams, working on the owner’s behalf. The page refused direct requests; its text was checked through a reader service. Used in Delegate an ongoing responsibility (persistent agents).
  60. OpenAI, Meet dots. Vendor documentation: a dot keeps track of an ongoing responsibility between conversations, uses plugins with the owner’s connected accounts and existing permissions, can start Work or Codex tasks, and passes actions through automatic review that lets it proceed, asks for approval or hands a step to the owner. Used in Delegate an ongoing responsibility (persistent agents).
  61. xAI, Use the computer and apps. Vendor documentation for Grok Bot: every bot on an account uses the same computer, with shared browser sign-ins and command-line credentials; each bot’s screen is not a separate security boundary. Used in Delegate an ongoing responsibility (persistent agents).
  62. Rick Blalock, Learnings from moving my Grok Bots to Devin Bots (17 November 2026). One practitioner’s beta account; not a controlled comparison. Reports that orchestration across sessions was the strongest part and that the engineering bots kept bringing him items to review. Used in Delegate an ongoing responsibility (persistent agents).
